questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a life process?

key_points: Life processes are maintenance functions performed by living organisms: nutrition, respiration, transportation, excretion
Decomposition is the breakdown of dead organic matter by external agents (microbes) — not a maintenance function of the organism itself
Trick to remember: if an organism does NOT perform it to keep itself alive, it is not a life process
rubric.expected_answer: Decomposition
rubric.hint: Think about which process is performed by an organism itself to stay alive.

questions.text: Why are life processes necessary for the maintenance of living organisms?

key_points: Living organisms need energy and materials for maintaining and repairing structures
Molecular movements needed for body organisation require life processes
rubric.expected_answer: Life processes such as nutrition, respiration, and excretion are necessary because living organisms constantly need energy to maintain their highly ordered body structures. These processes enable molecular movements required for maintaining organisation and repair of damaged parts.
rubric.hint: Consider what would happen inside cells if energy supply stopped permanently.

questions.text: The raw materials for photosynthesis are:

key_points: The two raw materials consumed in photosynthesis are CO2 (enters via stomata) and H2O (absorbed by roots)
Sunlight and chlorophyll are conditions/catalysts, not raw materials that get used up
Equation: 6CO2 + 6H2O + sunlight/chlorophyll produces C6H12O6 + 6O2
rubric.expected_answer: CO₂ and H₂O
rubric.hint: Think about what plants actually consume as raw materials versus what they produce.

questions.text: The site of photosynthesis in a cell is:

key_points: Chloroplasts are the organelles in plant cells where photosynthesis takes place
They contain the green pigment chlorophyll that absorbs light energy
Mitochondria perform respiration (energy release); do not confuse the two organelles
rubric.expected_answer: Chloroplast
rubric.hint: Recall which organelle contains the green pigment that captures light energy.

questions.text: Explain the role of stomata in photosynthesis.

key_points: Stomata are tiny pores on leaf surface regulated by guard cells
They allow CO₂ to enter the leaf for photosynthesis
They also facilitate transpiration
rubric.expected_answer: Stomata are tiny pores on the surface of leaves, controlled by guard cells. They allow carbon dioxide from the atmosphere to enter the leaf, which is essential for photosynthesis. Stomata also facilitate the release of oxygen and water vapour (transpiration).
rubric.hint: Think about how CO2 enters a leaf and what controls that entry point.

questions.text: Write the balanced chemical equation for photosynthesis.

key_points: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ in presence of sunlight and chlorophyll
rubric.expected_answer: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O  →(sunlight, chlorophyll)→  C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. Carbon dioxide and water, in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll, produce glucose and oxygen.
rubric.hint: Recall the balanced equation and identify what goes in on the left side.

questions.text: Describe the events occurring during photosynthesis.

key_points: Absorption of light energy by chlorophyll
Conversion of light energy to chemical energy and splitting of water
Reduction of CO₂ to carbohydrates
rubric.expected_answer: During photosynthesis three events occur: (i) Absorption of light energy by chlorophyll. (ii) Conversion of light energy to chemical energy, with the splitting of water molecules into hydrogen and oxygen. (iii) Reduction of carbon dioxide to carbohydrates using the chemical energy from step (ii).
rubric.hint: Think about the three key events: light absorption, water splitting, and CO2 fixation.

questions.text: Explain the process of nutrition in Amoeba with the help of a diagram. Name the steps involved.

key_points: Amoeba surrounds food particle using pseudopodia
Food vacuole is formed for digestion
Enzymes break down food inside the vacuole
Digested food is absorbed into cytoplasm
Undigested food is egested
rubric.expected_answer: Amoeba takes in food using temporary finger-like extensions called pseudopodia. The food particle is engulfed forming a food vacuole (ingestion). Digestive enzymes are secreted into the vacuole to break down complex substances into simpler ones (digestion). The digested food is then absorbed into the cytoplasm (absorption). Undigested residue is expelled from the body (egestion). The process is called holozoic nutrition.
rubric.hint: Think about the temporary extensions Amoeba forms and the steps from ingestion to egestion.

questions.text:
Study the given figure of a stomatal pore and answer the following questions:
(a) Identify parts labelled A (guard cell) and B (stomatal pore).
(b) State one function of stomata.
(c) What happens to the stomatal pore when guard cells lose water?

key_points: A is guard cell, B is stomatal pore
Stomata allow gas exchange for photosynthesis
When guard cells lose water they become flaccid and the pore closes
rubric.expected_answer: (a) A = Guard cell, B = Stomatal pore. (b) Stomata allow exchange of gases (CO₂ in, O₂ out) for photosynthesis and facilitate transpiration. (c) When guard cells lose water, they become flaccid (shrink), causing the stomatal pore to close.
rubric.hint: Consider what happens to guard cells when they lose water: turgid or flaccid?

questions.text: Draw a well-labelled diagram of the cross-section of a leaf showing the arrangement of cells involved in photosynthesis.

key_points: Upper and lower epidermis
Palisade mesophyll with chloroplasts
Spongy mesophyll
Stomata on lower epidermis
Vascular bundle (xylem and phloem)
rubric.expected_answer: Diagram should show: upper epidermis, palisade mesophyll (tightly packed, many chloroplasts), spongy mesophyll (loosely packed), lower epidermis with stomata, and vascular bundle.
rubric.hint: Recall the layers from upper to lower epidermis and where chloroplasts are densest.

questions.text: Organisms that obtain nutrition from dead and decaying organic matter are called:

key_points: Saprophytes feed on dead and decaying organic matter by secreting digestive enzymes externally
Examples: Rhizopus (bread mould), mushrooms, many soil bacteria
Distinction: parasites feed on living hosts; saprophytes feed on non-living dead matter
rubric.expected_answer: Saprophytes
rubric.hint: Think about which option feeds on non-living decaying matter, not a living host.

questions.text: Differentiate between saprophytic and parasitic mode of nutrition with one example each.

key_points: Saprophytic: nutrition from dead/decaying matter, e.g. mushroom/Rhizopus
Parasitic: nutrition from living host, causing harm, e.g. Cuscuta/tapeworm
rubric.expected_answer: Saprophytic nutrition involves obtaining nutrients from dead and decaying organic matter (e.g., Rhizopus/mushrooms). Parasitic nutrition involves deriving nutrients from a living host organism, often harming it (e.g., Cuscuta/tapeworm).
rubric.hint: Focus on where each organism gets nutrients from: dead matter vs. a living host.

questions.text: The function of hydrochloric acid in the stomach is to:

options.text: Create an acidic medium for pepsin and kill bacteria

key_points: HCl secreted in the stomach creates an acidic pH (~2) essential for the enzyme pepsin to work
HCl also kills most ingested bacteria, acting as a chemical barrier to infection
Starch is digested by salivary amylase in the mouth, not by HCl
rubric.expected_answer: Create an acidic medium for pepsin and kill bacteria
rubric.hint: Think about what HCl provides to the stomach environment for enzymes to function.

questions.text: The inner lining of the small intestine has numerous finger-like projections called:

key_points: Villi are finger-like projections lining the small intestine that massively increase surface area for absorption
Each villus contains blood capillaries and a lymph vessel (lacteal) for absorption of nutrients
Alveoli are in lungs; nephrons are in kidney — villi are exclusively in the small intestine
rubric.expected_answer: Villi
rubric.hint: Think about which structure increases surface area specifically for nutrient absorption.

questions.text: Why is the small intestine in herbivores longer than in carnivores?

key_points: Herbivores eat plant material containing cellulose which is harder to digest
Longer intestine provides more time and surface area for digestion
rubric.expected_answer: Herbivores eat plants that contain cellulose, which is difficult to digest. A longer small intestine provides more time and greater surface area for the complete digestion and absorption of this plant material. Carnivores eat meat, which is easier to digest, so they need a shorter intestine.
rubric.hint: Consider what makes cellulose harder to digest and why more intestine length helps.

questions.text: What is the role of saliva in the digestion of food?

key_points: Saliva contains salivary amylase enzyme
It breaks down starch into maltose sugar
Saliva also moistens food for easy swallowing
rubric.expected_answer: Saliva is secreted by salivary glands in the mouth. It contains the enzyme salivary amylase, which breaks down starch (a complex carbohydrate) into maltose (a simple sugar). Saliva also moistens the food, making it easier to swallow and facilitating the action of enzymes.
rubric.hint: Focus on which enzyme in saliva breaks down which substrate in the mouth.

questions.text: Explain the role of bile juice in digestion. Where is it produced and stored?

key_points: Bile juice is produced by the liver and stored in the gall bladder
It makes the medium alkaline for pancreatic enzymes
It emulsifies fats into smaller globules
rubric.expected_answer: Bile juice is produced by the liver and stored in the gall bladder. It plays two roles: (i) it makes the acidic food from the stomach alkaline so that pancreatic enzymes can act on it, and (ii) it emulsifies fats (breaks large fat globules into smaller ones) to increase the surface area for lipase to act.
rubric.hint: Think about bile's two roles: making the medium alkaline and breaking up fat globules.

questions.text: What is peristaltic movement? State its role in the alimentary canal.

key_points: Peristalsis is rhythmic contraction and relaxation of alimentary canal muscles
It pushes food forward through the digestive tract
rubric.expected_answer: Peristaltic movements are rhythmic contractions and relaxations of the muscles lining the alimentary canal. These wave-like movements push the food forward along the digestive tract, from the oesophagus to the rectum, ensuring that food moves through the canal even against gravity.
rubric.hint: Think about wave-like muscle contractions and their direction of movement along the canal.

questions.text: Describe the process of digestion in human beings, mentioning the role of digestive enzymes at each stage.

key_points: Mouth: salivary amylase converts starch to maltose
Stomach: HCl + pepsin digest proteins
Small intestine: bile emulsifies fats; trypsin + lipase act
Villi absorb digested food
Large intestine absorbs water
rubric.expected_answer: Digestion starts in the mouth where salivary amylase breaks starch into maltose. Food passes through the oesophagus by peristalsis to the stomach, where HCl creates an acidic medium and pepsin breaks proteins into peptides. In the small intestine, bile from the liver emulsifies fats, while pancreatic enzymes (trypsin, lipase, amylase) further digest proteins, fats, and carbohydrates. The intestinal wall secretes enzymes to complete digestion. Villi in the small intestine absorb the digested nutrients into the blood. The large intestine absorbs water from the undigested food, and the remainder is expelled.
rubric.hint: Trace each organ in order: mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine.

questions.text: During aerobic respiration, glucose is broken down into:

key_points: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen to completely oxidise glucose, producing CO2 and H2O with a large energy release
Equation: C6H12O6 + 6O2 produces 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy (38 ATP)
Ethanol+CO2 is produced by yeast (anaerobic); lactic acid by muscle cells (anaerobic) — not aerobic
rubric.expected_answer: CO₂ and H₂O
rubric.hint: Think about what aerobic respiration fully oxidises and what two by-products it makes.

questions.text: The end product of anaerobic respiration in yeast is:

key_points: In yeast without oxygen, anaerobic respiration incompletely breaks down glucose
Products are ethanol (alcohol) and CO2 — this is called fermentation
In human muscle cells, anaerobic respiration instead produces lactic acid (not ethanol)
rubric.expected_answer: CO₂ and ethanol
rubric.hint: Distinguish between yeast anaerobic and muscle cell anaerobic end products.

questions.text: What is the difference between aerobic and anaerobic respiration?

key_points: Aerobic: uses O₂, complete breakdown, produces CO₂ + H₂O + more energy
Anaerobic: without O₂, incomplete breakdown, produces ethanol/lactic acid + less energy
rubric.expected_answer: Aerobic respiration occurs in the presence of oxygen and results in complete breakdown of glucose into CO₂ and H₂O, releasing a large amount of energy. Anaerobic respiration occurs without oxygen and results in incomplete breakdown of glucose into ethanol and CO₂ (in yeast) or lactic acid (in muscles), releasing much less energy.
rubric.hint: Compare the role of oxygen and completeness of glucose breakdown in each type.

questions.text: Why does aerobic respiration release more energy than anaerobic respiration?

key_points: In aerobic respiration glucose is completely broken down into CO₂ and H₂O
In anaerobic respiration glucose is only partially broken down
rubric.expected_answer: Aerobic respiration releases more energy because glucose is completely oxidised into CO₂ and H₂O, extracting all the chemical energy stored in glucose. In anaerobic respiration, glucose is only partially broken down (into ethanol or lactic acid), so a significant amount of energy remains locked in the end products.
rubric.hint: Think about whether the end products of anaerobic respiration still contain stored energy.

questions.text: What is the role of the diaphragm and rib muscles in the process of breathing?

key_points: During inhalation: ribs move up and out, diaphragm flattens, volume increases
During exhalation: ribs move down and in, diaphragm rises, volume decreases
rubric.expected_answer: During inhalation, the diaphragm contracts and flattens while rib muscles contract to move ribs upward and outward. This increases the volume of the thoracic cavity, reducing pressure, and air rushes into the lungs. During exhalation, the diaphragm relaxes and curves upward, ribs move downward and inward, reducing the thoracic volume, and air is pushed out.
rubric.hint: Think about how diaphragm and rib movement change thoracic cavity volume during each phase.

questions.text: Why do we get muscle cramps after vigorous exercise?

key_points: During vigorous exercise oxygen supply is insufficient
Muscles respire anaerobically producing lactic acid
Accumulation of lactic acid causes cramps
rubric.expected_answer: During vigorous exercise, the demand for oxygen exceeds the supply. Muscle cells start respiring anaerobically, producing lactic acid as a by-product. The accumulation of lactic acid in the muscles causes cramps and fatigue.
rubric.hint: Think about what accumulates in muscles when oxygen supply is insufficient during exercise.

questions.text: During aerobic respiration, one molecule of glucose produces 38 molecules of ATP. If each ATP releases 30.5 kJ/mol of energy, calculate the total energy released per mole of glucose during aerobic respiration.

key_points: Aerobic respiration produces 38 ATP molecules per glucose molecule oxidised
Each ATP releases approximately 30.5 kJ/mol of usable energy
Total energy per mole of glucose = 38 x 30.5 = 1159 kJ/mol
rubric.expected_answer: Total energy = 38 × 30.5 = 1159 kJ/mol
rubric.hint: Multiply the number of ATP molecules by the energy released per molecule.

questions.text: Explain the mechanism of breathing in human beings. Describe what happens during inhalation and exhalation.

key_points: Inhalation: ribs up and out, diaphragm flattens, lung volume increases, air enters
Exhalation: ribs down and in, diaphragm curves up, lung volume decreases, air expelled
Gas exchange occurs at alveoli: O₂ to blood, CO₂ to alveoli
Alveoli provide large surface area for gas exchange
rubric.expected_answer: Breathing involves two phases. During inhalation, the intercostal muscles contract, moving ribs upward and outward; the diaphragm contracts and flattens. This increases the thoracic cavity volume, lowering air pressure inside the lungs, and atmospheric air rushes in. During exhalation, the intercostal muscles and diaphragm relax, reducing the thoracic cavity volume, increasing pressure, and pushing air out. In the lungs, air reaches the alveoli (tiny balloon-like structures with very thin walls and rich blood supply). Oxygen from alveolar air diffuses into blood capillaries, while CO₂ from blood diffuses into the alveoli to be exhaled. The extensive network of alveoli provides a large surface area (~80 m²) for efficient gas exchange.
rubric.hint: Cover both phases of breathing and describe gas exchange happening at the alveoli.

questions.text: Which blood vessel carries blood from the heart to the lungs?

key_points: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs for oxygenation
Pulmonary vein is the reverse — it returns oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium
Remember: arteries carry blood AWAY from the heart; veins carry blood TOWARDS the heart
rubric.expected_answer: Pulmonary artery
rubric.hint: Recall the rule that arteries carry blood away from the heart towards a destination.

questions.text: The blood component responsible for clotting is:

key_points: Platelets (thrombocytes) are tiny cell fragments that initiate blood clotting at wound sites
They release clotting factors that convert fibrinogen to fibrin, forming a mesh that seals wounds
RBCs carry oxygen; WBCs fight infections; plasma is the liquid matrix — none of these clot blood
rubric.expected_answer: Platelets
rubric.hint: Think about which blood component initiates the clotting process at a wound site.

questions.text: What is double circulation? Why is it necessary in human beings?

key_points: Blood passes through the heart twice in one complete cycle
Pulmonary circulation: heart → lungs → heart
Systemic circulation: heart → body → heart
Necessary to separate oxygenated and deoxygenated blood for efficient oxygen delivery
rubric.expected_answer: Double circulation means blood passes through the heart twice during one complete cycle. The right side of the heart pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs (pulmonary circulation), where it gets oxygenated. This oxygenated blood returns to the left side of the heart, which then pumps it to the rest of the body (systemic circulation). This separation ensures that oxygenated blood does not mix with deoxygenated blood, allowing efficient delivery of oxygen to tissues — essential for warm-blooded animals with high energy needs.
rubric.hint: Think about how many times blood passes through the heart and name the two loops.

questions.text: Differentiate between arteries and veins (any three differences).

key_points: Arteries have thick elastic walls; veins have thin walls
Arteries carry blood away from heart; veins carry blood towards heart
Arteries have no valves (except semilunar); veins have valves to prevent backflow
rubric.expected_answer: Arteries: (i) Thick, elastic walls to withstand high pressure. (ii) Carry oxygenated blood away from the heart (except pulmonary artery). (iii) No valves. Veins: (i) Thin walls with a larger lumen. (ii) Carry deoxygenated blood towards the heart (except pulmonary vein). (iii) Have valves to prevent backflow of blood.
rubric.hint: Compare wall thickness, presence of valves, and direction of blood flow in each vessel.

questions.text: What is lymph? State its two functions.

key_points: Lymph is a yellowish fluid formed when plasma leaks out of capillaries into intercellular spaces
It carries digested fats from the intestine
It provides immunity by carrying lymphocytes
rubric.expected_answer: Lymph (tissue fluid) is a yellowish fluid formed when plasma, proteins, and WBCs escape from capillaries into intercellular spaces. Functions: (i) It drains excess fluid from tissues back into the blood. (ii) It carries absorbed fats from the small intestine. (iii) Lymph nodes contain lymphocytes that fight infections, providing immunity.
rubric.hint: Think about where lymph comes from and how it relates to plasma leaking from capillaries.

questions.text: Why is the left ventricle of the heart thicker than the right ventricle?

key_points: Left ventricle pumps blood to entire body via systemic circulation
Needs to generate higher pressure to push blood over longer distances
rubric.expected_answer: The left ventricle has thicker muscular walls because it pumps oxygenated blood to the entire body through systemic circulation. This requires generating much higher pressure to push blood through the long network of arteries reaching all organs. The right ventricle only pumps blood to the nearby lungs (pulmonary circulation), requiring less pressure.
rubric.hint: Think about how far the left ventricle must pump blood compared to the right ventricle.

questions.text: Draw a diagram of the human heart and label the following parts: (i) Aorta (ii) Pulmonary artery (iii) Left ventricle (iv) Right atrium.

key_points: Four chambers clearly shown
Septum dividing left and right sides
Aorta arising from left ventricle
Pulmonary artery from right ventricle
Correct labelling of all four parts
rubric.expected_answer: Diagram of human heart showing four chambers (two atria, two ventricles), septum, aorta from left ventricle, pulmonary artery from right ventricle, pulmonary veins entering left atrium, vena cava entering right atrium. Labels: (i) Aorta (ii) Pulmonary artery (iii) Left ventricle (iv) Right atrium.
diagram_checklist: Septum dividing left and right sides
Correct labelling of all four parts
rubric.hint: Recall which vessel leaves from which ventricle and label all four required parts.

questions.text:
Assertion (A): Arteries have thick and elastic walls.
Reason (R): Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

key_points: Arteries receive blood pumped at high pressure directly from the ventricles of the heart
Thick, elastic walls allow arteries to expand under high pressure and then recoil without bursting
R correctly explains A: the high-pressure transport function is the reason for thick elastic walls
rubric.expected_answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. Arteries carry blood pumped from the heart at high pressure, so they need thick, elastic walls to withstand and maintain that pressure.
rubric.hint: Determine whether both statements are true and whether one explains the other causally.

questions.text: Water and minerals are transported in plants through:

key_points: Xylem is the vascular tissue that transports water and dissolved minerals from roots upward to leaves
Transport in xylem is unidirectional (upward only), driven mainly by transpiration pull
Phloem transports food (sucrose) from leaves to other parts — not water and minerals
rubric.expected_answer: Xylem
rubric.hint: Think about which vascular tissue transports water and minerals upward from roots.

questions.text: Explain the process of translocation in plants.

key_points: Translocation is the transport of food (sucrose) from leaves to other parts via phloem
Material is transferred into phloem using energy from ATP
This increases osmotic pressure, causing water to move into phloem
Pressure moves material through sieve tubes
rubric.expected_answer: Translocation is the transport of soluble products of photosynthesis (mainly sucrose) from leaves to other parts of the plant through the phloem. The food is loaded into sieve tubes of the phloem using energy from ATP. This increases the osmotic pressure in the phloem, causing water to enter from neighbouring xylem. The resulting pressure difference drives the movement of food through the sieve tubes to storage organs, growing regions, and roots.
rubric.hint: Think about how food is loaded into phloem using energy and what drives its movement.

questions.text: How does water move upward in tall trees against gravity?

key_points: Transpiration creates a suction pull at the top of xylem vessels
Cohesion of water molecules creates a continuous water column
Root pressure contributes to upward push from below
rubric.expected_answer: Water moves upward in tall trees primarily due to transpiration pull. As water evaporates from leaf surfaces through stomata, it creates a suction force that pulls the water column upward through xylem vessels. Cohesion (attraction between water molecules) and adhesion (attraction between water and xylem walls) maintain an unbroken water column. Root pressure also contributes by pushing water upward from the roots.
rubric.hint: Think about transpiration pull, cohesion of water molecules, and root pressure together.

questions.text: What is the role of transpiration in plants?

key_points: Creates suction pull for upward movement of water
Helps in absorption and transport of minerals
Cools the plant surface
rubric.expected_answer: Transpiration plays several roles: (i) It creates a transpiration pull (suction force) that helps draw water upward through xylem vessels. (ii) It aids in the absorption and upward transport of minerals dissolved in water from the soil. (iii) It has a cooling effect on the plant surface. (iv) It helps maintain the water balance in the plant.
rubric.hint: Consider how water loss from leaves creates a suction force driving upward water movement.

questions.text: A plant transpires 500 mL of water per day through its leaves. If only 2% of the water absorbed by roots is used in photosynthesis, calculate the total volume of water absorbed by the plant per day.

key_points: If 2% of absorbed water is used in photosynthesis, then 98% is transpired
Therefore: transpired water = 98% of total absorbed; rearrange to get total = transpired / 0.98
Calculation: 500 / 0.98 = approximately 510.2 mL total water absorbed per day
rubric.expected_answer: Water used in photosynthesis = 2% of total. Water transpired = 98% of total. So total = 500/0.98 ≈ 510.2 mL.
rubric.hint: If 2% is used in photosynthesis then 98% is transpired; rearrange to find total absorbed.

questions.text:
Assertion (A): Xylem transports water in an upward direction only.
Reason (R): Translocation of food in phloem can occur in both upward and downward directions.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

key_points: Xylem transport is unidirectional (only upward) because it is driven by transpiration pull from leaves
Phloem transport IS bidirectional, but this is a separate fact that does not explain xylem direction
Both A and R are TRUE, but R does NOT explain why xylem is unidirectional — hence option B
rubric.expected_answer: Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A. Xylem transport is unidirectional (upward) due to transpiration pull, while phloem transport is bidirectional. Both statements are true but the phloem fact does not explain why xylem is unidirectional.
rubric.hint: Check whether both statements are individually true and whether the second explains the first.

questions.text: The functional unit of the kidney is:

key_points: The nephron is the microscopic structural and functional unit of the kidney; each kidney has ~1 million nephrons
A nephron performs ultrafiltration, selective reabsorption, and secretion to produce urine
Neuron is a nerve cell; alveolus is in lungs; villus is in the small intestine
rubric.expected_answer: Nephron
rubric.hint: Think about which microscopic unit inside the kidney performs filtration and reabsorption.

questions.text: Describe the structure and functioning of a nephron.

key_points: Nephron has Bowman's capsule containing glomerulus (cluster of capillaries)
Blood is filtered under pressure in the glomerulus — filtration
Useful substances (glucose, amino acids, salts, water) are reabsorbed in the tubular part
Remaining fluid (urine) is collected in the collecting duct
rubric.expected_answer: A nephron is the structural and functional unit of the kidney. It consists of: (i) Bowman's capsule — a cup-shaped structure enclosing a cluster of capillaries called the glomerulus. Blood entering the glomerulus is filtered under high pressure (ultrafiltration). Water, glucose, amino acids, salts, and urea pass into the Bowman's capsule. (ii) A long tubular part where selective reabsorption occurs — useful substances like glucose, amino acids, and most water are reabsorbed into the blood capillaries. (iii) The remaining fluid (urine) containing urea, excess salts, and water passes into the collecting duct and eventually to the ureter.
rubric.hint: Trace the path: Bowman capsule and glomerulus for filtration, tubule for reabsorption.

questions.text: How do plants excrete their waste products?

key_points: Plants excrete O₂ and CO₂ through stomata during photosynthesis/respiration
Excess water removed by transpiration
Waste products stored in vacuoles, old xylem, bark, or shed as falling leaves
Some waste stored as resins and gums
rubric.expected_answer: Plants excrete waste products by various methods: (i) Gaseous wastes (O₂ and CO₂) are removed through stomata. (ii) Excess water is transpired through leaves. (iii) Many waste products are stored in cellular vacuoles, old xylem, bark, or in leaves that fall off. (iv) Some plants store wastes as resins and gums in old wood. Plants do not have specialised excretory organs like animals.
rubric.hint: Think about how plants use stomata, transpiration, leaves, and vacuoles for waste removal.

questions.text: The kidneys filter approximately 180 litres of blood plasma per day. If the normal urine output is 1.5 litres per day, calculate the percentage of filtrate that is reabsorbed by the renal tubules.

key_points: Kidney filters ~180 L of blood plasma per day, but only ~1.5 L is excreted as urine
Reabsorbed volume = total filtrate - urine = 180 - 1.5 = 178.5 L
Percentage reabsorbed = (178.5 / 180) x 100 = 99.17%, showing the extreme efficiency of tubular reabsorption
rubric.hint: Reabsorbed equals filtrate minus urine; divide by filtrate and multiply by 100.

questions.text: Draw a labelled diagram of the excretory system in human beings. Label: kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder, urethra.

key_points: Pair of kidneys shown at correct position
Ureters connecting kidneys to bladder
Urinary bladder below
Urethra from bladder
Renal artery and vein on each kidney
rubric.expected_answer: Diagram showing: pair of bean-shaped kidneys, renal arteries and veins, ureters descending from each kidney to the urinary bladder, and urethra leading out from the bladder.
diagram_checklist: Pair of kidneys shown at correct position
Renal artery and vein on each kidney
rubric.hint: Draw two kidneys with ureters leading to a bladder and a urethra exiting below.

questions.text: The basic criterion for considering something 'alive' is:

key_points: The defining feature of a living organism is continuous molecular movement and maintenance reactions inside cells
Growth alone is not unique to life (crystals grow); movement alone is not sufficient either
Maintenance reactions ensure organised body structures are preserved against natural breakdown
rubric.expected_answer: Molecular movement and maintenance reactions
rubric.hint: Think about what is happening inside cells even when the organism looks completely still.

questions.text: Why are maintenance processes necessary even when an organism is not doing anything visibly?

key_points: Even at rest, molecular movements and chemical reactions continue
Energy is needed to maintain body organisation and repair wear and tear
rubric.expected_answer: Even when organisms appear inactive, their internal molecular processes never stop. Continuous energy is required to maintain the organised structure of the body, repair damaged molecules and cells, and sustain essential chemical reactions. Without these maintenance processes, the ordered biological structures would break down.
rubric.hint: Consider what would break down inside cells if molecular maintenance reactions stopped.

questions.text: Which gas is released during photosynthesis?

key_points: During photosynthesis, water molecules are split (photolysis) and oxygen is released as a by-product through stomata
This photosynthetically produced oxygen is the main source of atmospheric O2 on Earth
CO2 is a reactant consumed during photosynthesis; it is only released during respiration
rubric.expected_answer: Oxygen
rubric.hint: Think about what is released when water molecules are split during the light reaction.

questions.text: The green pigment present in leaves that absorbs sunlight is:

key_points: Chlorophyll is the green photosynthetic pigment in chloroplasts that absorbs red and blue wavelengths of light
It reflects green light, which is why plants appear green to us
Haemoglobin carries oxygen in blood; xanthophyll and carotene are accessory/non-green pigments
rubric.expected_answer: Chlorophyll
rubric.hint: Think about which pigment reflects green light and absorbs sunlight for photosynthesis.

questions.text: Which of the following organisms is an autotroph?

key_points: Autotrophs manufacture their own food from inorganic raw materials using sunlight (photosynthesis) or chemical energy
Green plants are the principal autotrophs, converting CO2 and H2O into glucose via photosynthesis
Mushroom is a saprophyte; Amoeba is a holozoic heterotroph; Cuscuta is a parasitic plant — all heterotrophs
rubric.expected_answer: Green plant
rubric.hint: Think about which organism makes its own food using sunlight rather than consuming others.

questions.text: What is the function of guard cells in a leaf?

key_points: Guard cells regulate the opening and closing of stomata
When turgid they open the pore; when flaccid they close it
rubric.expected_answer: Guard cells are specialised kidney-shaped cells that surround each stomatal pore. They regulate the opening and closing of stomata. When guard cells absorb water and become turgid, the stomatal pore opens, allowing gas exchange. When they lose water and become flaccid, the pore closes.
rubric.hint: Think about what guard cells do when they absorb water versus when they lose water.

questions.text: Why do desert plants take up carbon dioxide at night?

key_points: Desert plants keep stomata closed during the day to prevent water loss
They open stomata at night to take in CO₂
rubric.expected_answer: Desert plants face extreme water scarcity. To minimise water loss through transpiration, they keep their stomata closed during the hot daytime. They open stomata at night when it is cooler, taking in CO₂ which is stored as an intermediate. This CO₂ is then used for photosynthesis during the day when sunlight is available.
rubric.hint: Think about how desert plants balance their need for CO2 against water loss.

questions.text: Name the enzyme present in saliva. What is its function?

key_points: Salivary amylase breaks down starch into maltose
rubric.expected_answer: The enzyme present in saliva is salivary amylase. It breaks down starch (a complex carbohydrate) into maltose (a simpler sugar) in the mouth.
rubric.hint: Recall the enzyme in saliva and the substrate it acts on in the mouth.

questions.text: If a plant produces 180 g of glucose through photosynthesis, calculate the mass of CO₂ consumed. (Molecular masses: C₆H₁₂O₆ = 180, CO₂ = 44)

key_points: From the balanced equation 6CO2 + 6H2O produces C6H12O6 + 6O2: one mole of glucose requires 6 moles of CO2
Moles of glucose produced = mass / molar mass = glucose_mass / 180
Mass of CO2 consumed = moles of glucose x 6 x 44 g/mol
rubric.expected_answer: Moles of glucose = 180/180 = 1 mol. From equation 6CO₂ needed per glucose. Mass CO₂ = 6 × 44 = 264 g.
rubric.hint: Use the balanced equation: 1 mole of glucose requires 6 moles of CO2.

questions.text: Villi are present in the:

key_points: Villi are microscopic finger-like projections found only on the inner wall of the small intestine
They enormously increase the absorptive surface area, enabling efficient uptake of digested nutrients
The small intestine is the primary site of both final digestion and absorption of all major food groups
rubric.expected_answer: Small intestine
rubric.hint: Think about which organ is specially adapted to maximise nutrient absorption surface area.

questions.text: The enzyme pepsin works in which medium?

key_points: Pepsin is a protease enzyme in the stomach that digests proteins into smaller peptides
It is only active in an acidic environment (pH ~2) created by HCl secreted by the stomach
Enzymes are pH-sensitive; pepsin becomes inactive in neutral or alkaline conditions
rubric.expected_answer: Acidic
rubric.hint: Think about the role HCl plays in creating the right environment for pepsin to work.

questions.text: Bile juice is stored in the:

key_points: Bile is produced by the liver but is stored in the gall bladder between meals
When fatty food enters the small intestine, the gall bladder contracts and releases bile into the duodenum
Remember: liver produces bile, gall bladder stores it — these are two different organs
rubric.expected_answer: Gall bladder
rubric.hint: Distinguish between where bile is produced and where it is stored between meals.

questions.text: What is the function of villi in the small intestine?

key_points: Villi increase the surface area for absorption of digested food
They have rich blood supply for efficient absorption
rubric.expected_answer: Villi are finger-like projections on the inner lining of the small intestine. They greatly increase the surface area available for absorption of digested food. Each villus has a network of blood capillaries and a lymph vessel (lacteal), enabling efficient absorption of nutrients into the bloodstream.
rubric.hint: Think about how finger-like projections increase surface area and what vessels they contain.

questions.text: What happens to food in the stomach?

key_points: Gastric glands secrete HCl, pepsin, and mucus
HCl makes medium acidic and kills bacteria
Pepsin digests proteins
Mucus protects stomach lining from acid
rubric.expected_answer: In the stomach, gastric glands in the walls secrete: (i) Hydrochloric acid (HCl) which creates an acidic medium (pH ~2) and kills ingested bacteria. (ii) Pepsin enzyme which breaks down proteins into smaller peptides. (iii) Mucus which protects the inner lining of the stomach from the corrosive effect of HCl.
rubric.hint: Think about the three secretions of gastric glands and what each one does.

questions.text: Why is the process of digestion necessary even though food contains complex nutrients?

key_points: Food contains large complex molecules that cannot be absorbed directly
Digestion breaks them into small soluble molecules that can pass through cell membranes
rubric.expected_answer: The food we eat contains complex, large, and insoluble molecules like starch, proteins, and fats. These molecules are too big to pass through the walls of the small intestine into the blood. Digestion breaks them down into smaller, simpler, and soluble molecules (like glucose, amino acids, and fatty acids) that can be absorbed and used by cells.
rubric.hint: Think about the size of food molecules compared to pores in the intestinal wall.

questions.text: The first step of glucose breakdown in all organisms occurs in the:

key_points: Glycolysis — the first step of respiration — occurs in the cytoplasm and breaks glucose into pyruvate
This is common to BOTH aerobic and anaerobic respiration in ALL organisms
Mitochondria are involved only in the subsequent aerobic steps (Krebs cycle and electron transport chain)
rubric.expected_answer: Cytoplasm
rubric.hint: Think about where glycolysis occurs and which step is common to both respiration types.

questions.text: Anaerobic respiration in muscles produces:

key_points: During vigorous exercise, muscles cannot get enough oxygen and switch to anaerobic respiration
In human muscle cells, anaerobic respiration produces lactic acid — not ethanol (which is yeast)
Accumulated lactic acid causes muscle fatigue and cramps; it is cleared when oxygen supply is restored
rubric.expected_answer: Lactic acid
rubric.hint: Distinguish between anaerobic products in yeast and in human muscle cells specifically.

questions.text: The organelle responsible for aerobic respiration is:

key_points: Mitochondria are the "powerhouse of the cell" where aerobic respiration occurs and most ATP is produced
The Krebs cycle and electron transport chain (ETC) take place in the mitochondria
Chloroplasts are for photosynthesis; glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm — not in mitochondria
rubric.expected_answer: Mitochondria
rubric.hint: Think about which organelle is called the powerhouse of the cell and why.

questions.text: What is the role of the nose in the respiratory system?

key_points: Hair and mucus in nostrils filter dust particles
Air is warmed and moistened before entering the lungs
rubric.expected_answer: The nose filters incoming air using fine hairs and mucus in the nostrils, trapping dust particles and pathogens. It also warms and moistens the air before it passes into the lungs, protecting the delicate lung tissues.
rubric.hint: Think about the two roles the nose plays before air reaches the delicate lung tissues.

questions.text: Why is it important to have a large surface area in the lungs?

key_points: Large surface area allows efficient exchange of O₂ and CO₂
Millions of alveoli provide approximately 80 m² surface area
rubric.expected_answer: Lungs need a very large surface area for efficient gas exchange. Millions of tiny alveoli provide approximately 80 m² of surface area in human lungs. This extensive area ensures that sufficient oxygen can diffuse into the blood and carbon dioxide can diffuse out during each breathing cycle, meeting the body's metabolic demands.
rubric.hint: Think about how millions of tiny alveoli contribute to efficient gas diffusion.

questions.text: Name the end products of anaerobic respiration in yeast. Mention one commercial application of this process.

key_points: Ethanol and CO₂ are the end products
Used in brewing/wine-making and baking
rubric.expected_answer: The end products of anaerobic respiration in yeast are ethanol (alcohol) and carbon dioxide. This process is called fermentation. Commercial applications include: brewing and wine-making (where ethanol is the desired product) and baking (where CO₂ causes dough to rise).
rubric.hint: Think about what yeast produces without oxygen and how bakers and brewers use this.

questions.text: If one molecule of glucose yields 38 ATP during aerobic respiration and only 2 ATP during anaerobic respiration, how many times more ATP is produced in aerobic respiration compared to anaerobic respiration?

key_points: Aerobic respiration yields 38 ATP per glucose; anaerobic respiration yields only 2 ATP per glucose
Aerobic / anaerobic ratio = 38 / 2 = 19 times more energy from aerobic respiration
This enormous difference explains why aerobic organisms can sustain much higher activity levels
rubric.expected_answer: 38 ÷ 2 = 19 times more ATP is produced in aerobic respiration.
rubric.hint: Divide aerobic ATP count by anaerobic ATP count to find the ratio.

questions.text: The liquid part of blood is called:

key_points: Blood has two parts: the liquid plasma (about 55% of blood volume) and the cellular components
Plasma is the yellowish fluid that transports nutrients, hormones, CO2, and proteins
Lymph is tissue fluid outside blood vessels; serum is plasma minus clotting factors
rubric.expected_answer: Plasma
rubric.hint: Think about the fluid component of blood that carries dissolved substances through vessels.

questions.text: Valves are present in:

key_points: Veins carry blood at lower pressure back towards the heart and contain valves to prevent backflow
The valves ensure one-way blood flow toward the heart against gravity in the limbs
Arteries have thick walls for high pressure but lack internal valves (except at heart exits)
rubric.expected_answer: Veins
rubric.hint: Think about which type of vessel needs valves to prevent backflow at low pressure.

questions.text: Which chamber of the heart receives oxygenated blood from the lungs?

key_points: Pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood from the lungs and deliver it to the left atrium of the heart
From the left atrium, oxygenated blood passes to the left ventricle, which pumps it to the body via the aorta
The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the body via the vena cava — opposite side
rubric.expected_answer: Left atrium
rubric.hint: Trace oxygenated blood from lungs back to the heart: which side and chamber receives it?

questions.text: Name the components of blood and state one function of each.

key_points: Plasma: transports nutrients, hormones, CO₂
RBC: carry oxygen using haemoglobin
WBC: fight infections
Platelets: help in blood clotting
rubric.expected_answer: Blood components: (i) Plasma — the fluid matrix that transports dissolved nutrients, hormones, proteins, and CO₂. (ii) Red blood cells (RBCs) — contain haemoglobin to transport oxygen. (iii) White blood cells (WBCs) — fight infections and provide immunity. (iv) Platelets — help in clotting of blood at wound sites to prevent blood loss.
rubric.hint: Name all four blood components and link each to one function: oxygen, immunity, clotting, transport.

questions.text: What would happen if there were no platelets in the blood?

key_points: Blood would not clot at wound sites
Even minor injuries could lead to continuous bleeding
rubric.expected_answer: If there were no platelets in the blood, the clotting mechanism would fail. At any site of injury, blood would not coagulate to seal the wound. This would result in continuous bleeding even from minor cuts, which could be life-threatening. Platelets release clotting factors that initiate the coagulation cascade to form a plug at wound sites.
rubric.hint: Think about what happens at a wound site if the clotting process cannot begin.

questions.text: Why is the separation of the right and left sides of the heart useful in mammals?

key_points: Prevents mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood
Ensures efficient oxygen delivery needed for maintaining body temperature
rubric.expected_answer: The separation of the right and left sides of the heart by the septum prevents the mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood. This ensures that highly oxygenated blood is delivered to the body tissues, which is essential for the high energy demands of warm-blooded mammals who need to maintain constant body temperature.
rubric.hint: Think about why mixing oxygenated and deoxygenated blood reduces oxygen delivery efficiency.

questions.text: Food is transported in plants through:

key_points: Phloem is the vascular tissue that transports dissolved food (mainly sucrose) from leaves to all other parts of the plant
This process is called translocation and requires energy from ATP
Xylem transports water and minerals upward — never food
rubric.expected_answer: Phloem
rubric.hint: Think about which vascular tissue transports the products of photosynthesis from leaves.

questions.text: The process of loss of water from leaves in the form of vapour is called:

key_points: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from plant surfaces, mainly through stomata in leaves
It creates a transpiration pull (suction) that helps draw water upward through xylem
Translocation is food movement through phloem; osmosis is water movement across membranes
rubric.expected_answer: Transpiration
rubric.hint: Think about the term for water leaving leaves as vapour through stomata.

questions.text: Differentiate between xylem and phloem based on their function.

key_points: Xylem transports water and minerals upward from roots to leaves
Phloem transports food from leaves to other parts in both directions
rubric.expected_answer: Xylem transports water and dissolved minerals from roots upward to leaves and other aerial parts. This transport is unidirectional. Phloem transports the products of photosynthesis (mainly sucrose) from leaves to storage organs, roots, and growing parts. Phloem transport (translocation) is bidirectional.
rubric.hint: Compare direction and substance transported in xylem versus phloem.

questions.text: How do root cells absorb water from the soil?

key_points: Root hair cells have higher solute concentration than soil water
Water moves into root cells by osmosis along concentration gradient
rubric.expected_answer: Root hair cells have a higher concentration of dissolved substances (ions, sugars) compared to the soil water. Water from the soil moves into the root hair cells by osmosis — from a region of higher water concentration (soil) to lower water concentration (cell sap). This water then moves from cell to cell across the root cortex to the xylem vessels.
rubric.hint: Think about osmosis: which side has higher solute concentration, root cells or soil water?

questions.text: A plant absorbs water at a rate of 25 mL per hour through its roots. How much water (in litres) will it absorb in 12 hours?

key_points: Water absorption rate = 25 mL per hour; time = 12 hours
Total water absorbed = rate x time = 25 x 12 = 300 mL
Convert to litres: 300 mL / 1000 = 0.30 L
rubric.hint: Multiply rate by time, then convert millilitres to litres.

questions.text: Urea is formed in the:

key_points: Urea is the main nitrogenous excretory waste in humans, formed in the liver by deamination of excess amino acids
The kidneys then filter urea from the blood to form urine — but urea is MADE in the liver, not the kidneys
Deamination: amino group (-NH2) removed from amino acids and converted to urea in the liver
rubric.expected_answer: Liver
rubric.hint: Think about which organ converts excess amino acids to urea via deamination.

questions.text: The tubular structure connecting the kidney to the urinary bladder is the:

key_points: Ureters are two tubes (one from each kidney) that carry urine down to the urinary bladder
Urethra is a single tube that carries urine from the bladder to the outside during urination
Memory tip: UreteR goes to the bladdeR; urethRa exits the body (different tube)
rubric.expected_answer: Ureter
rubric.hint: Think about which tube connects each kidney to the urinary bladder, not the urethra.

questions.text: What is the role of the kidneys in the human body?

key_points: Kidneys filter blood to remove nitrogenous waste (urea, uric acid)
They regulate water and salt balance in the body
rubric.expected_answer: The kidneys are the main excretory organs in humans. They filter blood to remove nitrogenous waste products (mainly urea and uric acid) along with excess water and salts. The filtered waste is expelled as urine. Kidneys also play a vital role in regulating water and electrolyte balance (osmoregulation) in the body.
rubric.hint: Think about the kidney's two main jobs: filtering nitrogenous waste and regulating water balance.

questions.text: If the kidneys produce 1.5 litres of urine from 180 litres of filtrate in a day, what volume (in litres) of filtrate is reabsorbed?

key_points: Total filtrate per day = 180 L; urine produced = 1.5 L
Reabsorbed volume = 180 - 1.5 = 178.5 L
Renal tubules reabsorb useful substances (glucose, amino acids, water, salts) back into the blood
rubric.expected_answer: Reabsorbed volume = 180 - 1.5 = 178.5 litres.
rubric.hint: Subtract urine volume from total filtrate to find the volume reabsorbed.

questions.text: Cuscuta is an example of a:

key_points: Cuscuta (dodder) has no chlorophyll and cannot photosynthesise, so it lives as a parasite on host plants
It wraps around a host plant and inserts haustoria (sucking organs) to extract water and nutrients
Parasites harm their living host; saprophytes feed on non-living dead matter — Cuscuta does the former
rubric.expected_answer: Parasite
rubric.hint: Think about whether Cuscuta can photosynthesise and what kind of host it depends on.

questions.text: What is the mode of nutrition in fungi like bread mould (Rhizopus)?

key_points: Rhizopus shows saprophytic nutrition
It secretes enzymes onto dead organic matter and absorbs dissolved nutrients
rubric.expected_answer: Bread mould (Rhizopus) shows saprophytic mode of nutrition. It secretes digestive enzymes onto the dead organic matter (like bread), breaking it down into simpler soluble substances outside its body. These digested nutrients are then absorbed through the cell surface. This is also called extracellular digestion.
rubric.hint: Think about how Rhizopus digests food outside its body before absorbing it.

questions.text: Which of the following is the BEST definition of a life process?

options.text: Any chemical reaction occurring inside a cell
A maintenance function necessary to prevent damage and breakdown in the body
Movement of an organism from one place to another
Growth and reproduction of an organism

key_points: Life processes are maintenance functions carried out by all living organisms to prevent damage and breakdown.
They require energy (from nutrition) and maintain the organized complexity that defines life.
Without life processes, molecular damage would accumulate and the organism would die.
rubric.expected_answer: Option B — A maintenance function necessary to prevent damage and breakdown in the body.
rubric.hint: Think about which definition focuses on maintenance and preventing breakdown in the body.

questions.text: A doctor tests whether a person is alive by checking for breathing and heartbeat. Which two life processes do breathing and heartbeat represent, respectively?

key_points: Breathing is part of the respiration process — taking in O2 and releasing CO2 for cellular energy production.
Heartbeat drives the circulatory system which performs transportation — moving nutrients, gases, and waste around the body.
These two are used clinically as signs of life because they stop immediately at death.
rubric.expected_answer: Option B — Respiration (breathing) and Transportation (heartbeat/circulation).
rubric.hint: Think about which life process breathing links to and which process keeps the heart pumping.

questions.text: Carbon and oxygen are key elements needed by living organisms. From which life process do organisms primarily get carbon (as CO2) to build organic molecules?

options.text: Respiration releases CO2; autotrophs fix it via Nutrition (photosynthesis)

key_points: CO2 from the atmosphere is the carbon source for autotrophs.
Through photosynthesis (autotrophic nutrition), plants fix CO2 into glucose and other organic molecules.
Heterotrophs obtain carbon by consuming other organisms, ultimately tracing back to photosynthesis.
rubric.expected_answer: Option B — Autotrophs fix atmospheric CO2 through photosynthesis (autotrophic nutrition).
rubric.hint: Think about how autotrophs capture atmospheric CO2 to build organic molecules.

questions.text: Why is it said that all the activities of life processes are ultimately dependent on nutrition?

key_points: All life processes — respiration, transportation, excretion, reproduction — require energy.
Energy for cellular work comes from the oxidation of food molecules (obtained through nutrition).
Without nutrition, there is no fuel to drive the molecular movements that maintain organisation and prevent breakdown.
Therefore nutrition is the foundational life process on which all others depend.
rubric.expected_answer: All life processes require energy. Energy is obtained by breaking down food molecules (nutrition). Without nutrition, there is no energy to drive respiration, transportation, excretion, or any other maintenance process, so the organism would die.
rubric.hint: Think about where the energy for every other life process ultimately comes from.

questions.text: Which of the following organisms is an example of a saprotrophic (saprophytic) heterotroph?

key_points: Saprotrophic organisms feed on dead and decaying organic matter by secreting digestive enzymes outside their body (extracellular digestion) and absorbing the products.
Bread mould (Rhizopus) is a classic example — it grows on bread and secretes amylase and other enzymes.
Amoeba is holozoic; pitcher plant is insectivorous; tapeworm is parasitic.
rubric.expected_answer: Option B — Bread mould (Rhizopus) is a saprotrophic fungus that digests dead organic matter externally.
rubric.hint: Think about which organism feeds on dead organic matter by secreting enzymes externally.

questions.text: In Amoeba, food is engulfed by pseudopodia to form a food vacuole. What are the correct steps of holozoic nutrition in the correct order?

key_points: Holozoic nutrition involves five steps in order: Ingestion (taking in food) -> Digestion (breaking down complex molecules) -> Absorption (nutrients enter cells) -> Assimilation (using nutrients for energy/growth) -> Egestion (removing undigested waste).

In Amoeba, pseudopodia engulf food (ingestion), digestive enzymes break it down in the food vacuole (digestion), nutrients diffuse into cytoplasm (absorption + assimilation), and undigested matter is expelled (egestion).
rubric.expected_answer: Option A — Ingestion -> Digestion -> Absorption -> Assimilation -> Egestion.
rubric.hint: Recall the correct sequence from taking food in to expelling undigested waste.

questions.text: How does a parasitic plant like Cuscuta (dodder) obtain its nutrition? How does this differ from a saprotrophic organism?

key_points: Cuscuta (dodder) is a parasitic plant — it lacks chlorophyll and winds around a host plant.
It sends haustorial roots into the host's vascular tissue (xylem and phloem) and directly absorbs water, minerals, and prepared food from the living host.
Saprotrophic organisms feed on DEAD and decaying organic matter by secreting digestive enzymes externally.
Key difference: Parasite feeds on a LIVING host; saprophyte feeds on DEAD organic matter.
rubric.expected_answer: Cuscuta is a parasite: it uses haustoria to tap into a living host plant's vascular tissue and steal nutrients. Saprophytes (like fungi) secrete enzymes to digest DEAD organic matter externally then absorb the products. Parasite = living host; Saprophyte = dead matter.
rubric.hint: Focus on whether each organism feeds on a living host or dead decaying matter.

questions.text: Why are heterotrophs dependent on autotrophs for their energy needs? Explain with reference to the flow of energy in an ecosystem.

key_points: Autotrophs (plants, algae) convert solar energy into chemical energy stored in organic molecules via photosynthesis.
Heterotrophs cannot make their own food — they must consume other organisms to obtain organic molecules.
When heterotrophs eat autotrophs or other heterotrophs, they break down these organic molecules to release the stored energy.
Energy flows from sun -> autotrophs -> herbivores -> carnivores; at each step, energy is lost as heat.
Ultimately, all energy in an ecosystem originates from autotrophic fixation of solar energy.
rubric.expected_answer: Autotrophs fix solar energy into organic molecules via photosynthesis. Heterotrophs cannot do this, so they must consume autotrophs (or other heterotrophs) to obtain organic molecules for energy. Energy flows: Sun -> Autotrophs -> Heterotrophs, making heterotrophs fundamentally dependent on autotrophs.
rubric.hint: Think about where autotrophs get energy from and why heterotrophs cannot do the same.
